text: cytosine.1-3 Amphotericin B may be given alone in patients unable to tolerate flucytosine. In re- fractory cases, amphotericin B may be given intrathecally or intraventricularly. Oral fluconazole and intravenous flu- cytosine is an alternative to the use of amphotericin B but carries a high risk of toxicity. After induction, oral flucona- zole should be given as consolidation therapy; if flucona- zole cannot be given, itraconazole is a suitable though less effective alternative.1-3 Immunocompetent patients with CNS disease and immu- nocompromised patients (without HIV infection) may re- quire 6 to 12 months of suppressive therapy with oral flu- conazole after a primary course of antifungal therapy.1 HIV-infected patients should generally receive lifelong maintenance therapy,1-4 although it may be possible to stop secondary prophylaxis in patients who exhibit a sustained response to highly active antiretroviral therapy and who remain asymptomatic with regard to cryptococcosis. US guidelines4 recommend restarting secondary prophylaxis if the CD4+ T lymphocyte count falls below 100 to 200 cells/microlitre. Primary prophylaxis in patients with HIV infection is not generally recommended since it has not been shown to be more beneficial than treating cryptococcal infections when they occur and may increase the risk of resistance.4 1.
